nameStory: The 'small green wood orchid' name tells you exactly what you're looking for - a tiny, greenish orchid hiding in the woods! The scientific name 'clavellata' means 'club-shaped,' referring to the distinctive swollen tip of the flower's spur that looks like a little club. It's also called the club-spur orchid for this same clubby feature.
description: This is one of New England's most subtle native orchids, standing just 6-20 inches tall with a single slender spike of tiny yellowish-green flowers. Unlike the showy orchids you might imagine, this woodland gem is incredibly modest, with flowers so small and green they almost disappear among the forest vegetation. Each plant typically has just one oval leaf partway up the stem, though sometimes there's a smaller leaf higher up. The whole plant has an almost grass-like appearance until you look closely at those unmistakably orchid-shaped flowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers arranged in a loose spike, each with a distinctive club-shaped spur that swells at the tip like a little paddle - this clubby spur is the dead giveaway

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Usually just one main oval leaf positioned about halfway up the stem, smooth to the touch and unremarkable green color, sometimes with a smaller bract-like leaf higher up

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, single-stemmed plant standing 6-20 inches tall, often looking almost grass-like from a distance until you notice the flower spike

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers have no fragrance that humans can detect, and the greenish color makes them blend in perfectly with surrounding vegetation

habitat: Look for this secretive orchid in moist, acidic woods and boggy areas throughout New England, especially in sphagnum moss or wet sandy soils. It favors the edges of swamps, wet meadows, and coniferous forests where the soil stays consistently damp. You'll often find it growing alongside other bog plants like pitcher plants, sundews, and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge from the ground as single stems with developing leaves. The plant is building energy but not yet flowering.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from July through August, when the tiny green flowers are at their peak and most identifiable. This is the best time to spot this elusive orchid.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to die back, becoming nearly impossible to locate as it blends with dying vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant underground with no visible parts above ground - impossible to find during this season.

funFact: This tiny orchid is so specialized that it relies on fungal partnerships in the soil to survive - without the right fungi literally feeding its roots, the plant cannot live, making it impossible to transplant or grow in gardens.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be overlooked entirely rather than confused with other plants, since the tiny green flowers are so inconspicuous they're easily mistaken for grass or sedge flower heads. The club-shaped spur is the key feature that screams 'orchid!' once you know to look for it.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the same family as tropical orchids sold in stores, this humble native couldn't be more different - it's evolved to be nearly invisible in its woodland home rather than showy and attention-grabbing.
compareHints: Among its bog orchid relatives, this is by far the smallest and most inconspicuous - while cousins like the fringed orchids have showy white or purple flowers, the small green wood orchid is all about stealth. The club-shaped spur is unique among New England's Platanthera orchids, making it instantly identifiable once you spot those tiny flowers. Unlike the round-leaved bog orchid which has two large basal leaves, this species typically has just one small leaf partway up the stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Platanthera relatives, the White-fringed Orchid is distinguished by its pure white color and deeply fringed petals - the Lesser and Greater Purple Fringed Orchids have similar fringed flowers but are purple, while other white bog orchids lack the dramatic fringe.
Among New England's bog orchids (Platanthera), the Lesser Purple Fringed Orchid is distinguished by its bright purple color and deeply fringed flower lips.
White bog orchid stands out from its Platanthera relatives by its pure white color and incredibly strong clove-like fragrance.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the ragged fringed orchid stands out for its greenish-white color and extremely irregular, deeply cut fringes.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the Greater Purple Fringed Orchid stands out for its size and deeply fringed purple petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this species is distinguished by its greenish-white flowers and self-fertilizing habit.
Among its bog orchid relatives, green bog orchid is distinguished by its consistently greenish flowers and preference for the wettest habitats.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the Round-leaved Bog Orchid is unique for having just two large, circular basal leaves.
Among New England's bog orchids, pale green orchid stands out for its particularly subtle coloring and preference for disturbed shoreline habitats.

Among New England's bog orchids, Hooker's is distinctive for having exactly two large basal leaves lying flat on the ground, while most other Platanthera species have multiple leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, Large-leaved Bog Orchid is unmistakable due to its two massive basal leaves - most other Platanthera species have smaller, more numerous leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the orange-fringed orchid is the only one with orange flowers and deeply fringed petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this is the only one with such intensely bright orange flowers in a dense, compact cluster.

Unlike its relatives the round-leaved bog orchid (which has two large round leaves) or Hooker's orchid (which has two broad leaves that hug the ground), the blunt-leaved rein orchid typically has just one distinctively paddle-shaped leaf with a rounded tip.
Among its Platanthera relatives, Shriver's frilly orchid is distinguished by its particular fringe pattern and purple coloration.
